title: What Must a Quantum-Memory Decoder Know About Temporally Correlated Noise?
authors: Danesh Morales-Hashemi, Graeme Smith, Ningping Cao
abstract: What must a quantum error-correction decoder know about temporally correlated noise, and what does it cost to learn? We study this question for fixed stabilizer memory experiments with known system-environment interactions. We formulate calibration in terms of the fidelity differences that select a Pauli recovery and relate missing information to the resulting fidelity loss. Our main example uses weak coherent $X$ rotations in a class of CSS codes including Shor, Steane, and odd-distance rotated surface codes. All physical qubits share a sign either fixed throughout a run or independently redrawn each interval. The two models have identical syndrome statistics and the same spatiotemporal Pauli process (SPP), obtained by Pauli-twirling every noise interval. Yet at suitable storage times, they require different logical corrections. In the weak-noise limit, each model is almost perfectly correctable when known. Without model information, even the best final recovery has a worst-case fidelity loss approaching $1/2$ relative to the noise-aware optimum, despite access to the full syndrome record. For this pair of models, at fixed code and fixed positive target loss below $1/2$, we prove matching calibration bounds. With logical preparation and final readout, complete QEC cycles require a number of noise intervals scaling as the inverse rotation angle raised to the code's $X$ distance. Allowing two uninterrupted intervals before one extraction reduces the optimal cost to inverse-square scaling. Physical Pauli twirling of every noise interval changes both recovery performance and its information requirements. Discarding the record of applied random Pauli operations makes the SPP sufficient for optimal recovery. Keeping this record can improve the attainable fidelity, but reaching that optimum may require additional noise information.
summary: This paper analyzes the theoretical requirements for quantum error-correcting decoders operating under temporally correlated noise. It compares two noise models—one with a fixed global sign and one with independently resampled signs—showing that while their syndrome statistics match, their optimal recovery strategies differ. The work establishes scaling laws for the required experimental resources (calibration) to maintain high fidelity.
main_problem: The paper investigates what information about temporally correlated noise a quantum error-correction (QEC) decoder must possess to achieve optimal recovery, and quantifies the cost of learning this information.
main_result: The optimal cost for complete QEC cycles scales inversely with the rotation angle raised to the code's X distance, and the authors prove matching calibration bounds for two different noise models (fixed vs. resampled signs).
method: The analysis uses a statistical decision theory framework, formulating calibration in terms of fidelity differences and employing process tensors to model the full quantum evolution.
model_or_system: The study uses fixed stabilizer memory experiments with CSS codes (e.g., Shor, Steane, surface codes) subjected to weak coherent X rotations, comparing two noise models: one where all qubits share a fixed sign, and one where the sign is redrawn independently each interval.
key_observables: Entanglement fidelity ($F$), fidelity loss ($\Delta F$), syndrome record ($y$), and the logical rotation accumulated over time.
important_parameters: The noise correlation structure (fixed vs. resampled signs), the code's X distance ($d_X$), and the rotation angle ($	heta$).
main_assumptions: The analysis assumes the ability to characterize the noise process via syndrome measurements and uses the Spatiotemporal Pauli Process (SPP) as a complete description for randomized errors.
figures_summary: Figure 1 illustrates the memory experiment flow, detailing the sequence from encoding, noise intervals, syndrome measurement, correction, and final recovery, alongside calibration runs.
paper_structure: The paper develops a general framework using process tensors to describe the logical instrument, then focuses on comparing the performance and required calibration data for different noise models (F vs. R) to determine the minimum information needed for optimal decoding.
why_interesting: It provides rigorous theoretical bounds on the information required to mitigate complex, time-dependent noise in quantum memory, which is crucial for scaling up quantum computation.
